metadata.title: The Routine Content Of Occupations: New Cross-Country Measures Based On PIAAC

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses OECD PIAAC microdata (2011–2012 wave) to construct a Routine Intensity Indicator (RII) from four PIAAC task-planning/flexibility questions, then aggregates individuals to 3-digit ISCO08 occupations using median RII values and forms routine-intensity quartiles. For the descriptive employment shares shown in Figure 1, the authors explicitly state that reweighted employment figures are used to ensure representativeness, but they do not report the specific PIAAC weight variable name in the excerpt provided. The analysis also discards unemployed respondents (because key RII components are absent) and excludes employed respondents with missing answers on any of the four RII components, which is a form of complete-case restriction for the index construction. No replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is described in the provided text, and the paper does not present student-level ML models where complex-survey weights would be required for predictive inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the study does not model cognitive achievement outcomes from PIAAC; instead, it constructs an occupation-level routine-intensity measure (RII) from Likert-frequency responses to task-planning and task-sequencing questions and then relates routine intensity to other skill proxies and employment patterns. Missing-data handling is implemented for the index components by discarding respondents with missing answers on any of the four RII questions, so the missing-data strategy is described rather than omitted.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses OECD PIAAC microdata for 22 OECD countries, but the analysis retains only employed respondents who provide information on occupation and/or sector. Unemployed respondents are discarded because the “sequentiability” and “flexibility” questions are absent for them. Self-employed individuals are kept. Respondents are excluded if they have missing information for at least one of the four RII components (Sequentiability, Flexibility, Plan_own, Organise_own), to avoid artificially low RII values due to missing answers. The resulting analytic sample for RII construction is 105,526 individuals (with 9,373 interviewed in Australia and Finland combined, as reported).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD paper constructs a new cross-country measure of the routine content of occupations using OECD PIAAC (2011–2012). It defines a Routine Intensity Indicator (RII) from four PIAAC questions capturing how frequently workers can modify task sequences, change task content, and plan/organise their own work. The authors compute individual RII values, then assign occupations to routine-intensity quartiles (high, medium, low, non-routine) using median RII values at the 3-digit ISCO08 level, with country-specific classifications for a subset of countries and pooled-data classification where needed. They report that, on average, 46% of employed persons work in non-routine (18%) or low routine-intensive (28%) occupations, with substantial cross-country variation. They also find a negative but not very strong relationship between routine intensity and workforce skill proxies (including numeracy skills), and they use the routine classification to describe employment resilience patterns over the business cycle, finding routine-intensive occupations are generally less resilient than non-routine occupations.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a descriptive measurement and cross-country comparison paper rather than an empirical predictive ML study: it does not train or evaluate supervised ML models on student-level outcomes, and it does not report PV-based achievement modeling. Consequently, fields required for predictive ML (e.g., main_findings structured as dataset→input→target→output prediction results) are intentionally left empty, while the outcome_summary captures the index construction and descriptive correlations/associations reported. The paper’s core methodological contribution is the construction of the RII and its application to occupation/sector classification and employment patterns.
